title: Numerals, and nominal forms in review

objectives.can: Read the numerals of Daniel and Ezra, and parse any noun for gender, number and state.

explanation.summary: The numbers of the Aramaic of the Bible are few, but they carry a rule that surprises learners: from three to ten, the form of the number has the opposite gender to the thing counted. This lesson also reviews the noun: its gender, its number, and its three states, which you need for every sentence you read.

sections.heading: The numbers that occur
body: Only some numbers occur in the texts. There are one, two, three, four, six, seven and ten; twenty, thirty and sixty; a hundred, a thousand, and the 'myriad' (ten thousand). Five, eight, nine, forty, fifty, seventy and the rest do not occur, so there is nothing to say about them. Two hundred occurs once, with a dual ending (EZR.6.17).

Numbers join with ו, largest first, as in the English 'a hundred and twenty': מְאָה וְעֶשְׂרִין (Daniel 6:2). The numbers eleven to nineteen are made by setting the unit before עֲשַׂר: תְּרֵי עֲשַׂר 'twelve' (Daniel 4:26). The word עִדָּן 'time' is tagged as a number in one verse; that is a slip in the analysis, and it is not a numeral.

Numbers can take the determined ending like nouns: אַלְפָּא 'the thousand' (Daniel 5:1). A number can come before or after the thing counted. The texts have both: אַרְבְּעָה גֻּבְרִין 'four men' (Daniel 3:25), and תּוֹרִין מְאָה 'a hundred bulls' (Ezra 6:17).

sections.heading: The rule of opposite gender
body: For the numbers three to ten there are two forms. One has a final -ָה or -ָא (תְּלָתָה, אַרְבְּעָה, עַשְׂרָה); the other has none (תְּלָת, אַרְבַּע, עֲשַׂר, שֵׁת). The short form goes with a feminine noun, and the form with the ending goes with a masculine noun. The number takes the opposite gender to the noun counted.

Daniel 7:24 shows both in one verse. The horns are feminine, and the verse has עֲשַׂר beside them. The kings are masculine, and the verse has עַשְׂרָה beside them. In the same way Daniel 7:3 has אַרְבַּע חֵיוָן 'four beasts' (feminine, short form), and Daniel 7:6 has אַרְבְּעָה רֵאשִׁין 'four heads' (masculine, form with the ending).

The corpus often marks a numeral as common gender, and it sometimes disagrees with the rule. Do not rely on the Gender feature of the number. Look at the noun it counts. The numbers one and two are different: they agree with the noun in the usual way (חַד with masculine, חֲדָה with feminine).

sections.heading: Dates and measures
body: Aramaic does not have a separate form for 'third' or 'sixth' in these texts. A date is a noun followed by a plain number. 'On the third day of Adar' is י֥וֹם תְּלָתָה in Ezra 6:15, and 'in the sixth year' is שְׁנַת שֵׁת in the same verse. 'In the second year' is שְׁנַת תַּרְתֵּין in Ezra 4:24. The corpus tags these three numbers as adjectives with the feature NumType=Ord, and it calls them 'ordinals'. They are the numbers you already know used in apposition.

A measure is a noun with its number: 'sixty cubits' and 'six cubits' in Daniel 3:1, with the short form שִׁת for a feminine noun 'cubit'. Gifts for the Temple in Ezra 6:17 and 7:22 are counted in the same way, in hundreds.

sections.heading: Nouns in review: gender and number
body: An Aramaic noun has a gender, masculine or feminine, and a number: singular, plural, and, for a few paired things, dual (רַגְלַיִן 'feet' in Daniel 7:4). Gender is not always visible: מֶלֶךְ 'king' ends in no letter that marks it, and מִלָּה 'word' is feminine. A few nouns are both. The corpus marks the gender it finds and sometimes writes 'common'.

The usual endings are a masculine plural -ִין, and a feminine plural -ָן in the absolute state. A feminine singular often ends in -ָה (absolute) or -ַת (construct). But nouns do not all follow the pattern: some masculine nouns have a feminine plural, and some feminine nouns a masculine one. The corpus's own label is the safe guide.

sections.heading: Nouns in review: the three states
body: The state of a noun says how it stands in its phrase. The determined (emphatic) state ends in -ָא and corresponds to 'the': מַלְכָּא 'the king'. The absolute state is the plain form: מַלְכִין 'kings'. The construct state is the form of a noun that is followed by the noun that owns it: מֶלֶךְ מַלְכַיָּא 'king of kings' (Daniel 2:37), where the first מֶלֶךְ is construct and the second is plural determined.
Compare the full set of one masculine and one feminine noun. Each form below stands in the texts.

misunderstandings: A number with a final -ָה is not a feminine number for a feminine noun: it is the reverse. The ending goes with a masculine noun.
The Gender feature on a numeral in the corpus is not a guide to the rule. Read the noun beside the number.
A date uses the same number as a count. תְּלָתָה in 'day three' is not a different word from the three of 'three men'.
The determined state is not always a plain 'the'. Names, and nouns that are already defined by what follows, may stand in other states. The state tells you the form, not the English article.

deeper.heading: Why the opposite gender?
body: The same rule exists in Hebrew and in other Semitic languages. One explanation is that the number from three to ten was originally an abstract noun (a 'threesome') with the feminine ending, and that the construction followed from it. The learner can leave the history aside: the rule is regular in the texts.
